Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-19
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Nina Patel (Redwood AE), Evan Rodriguez (Redwood SE), Samir Cho (Redwood SE), Claire Martin (Mercantile SecOps), Jamal Ortiz (Mercantile Infra), Alex Wei (Mercantile Compliance)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
- Purpose: deep dive on private/VPC access model, ingress/egress gating, KMS integration and audit log provenance for SOC 2 readiness.
- High-level outcome: alignment on egress-proxy pattern, preference for private control plane with strict RBAC + SSO, need for KMS HSM-backed key rotation plan and evidence collection points for audits.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Nina (Redwood AE): Hey everyone thanks for making time, I think we've got an hour plus here so we'll go deep on the access and egress patterns, and make sure we cover the SOC2 and K M S questions. Claire, Jamal, Alex, are you all good on audio?
[00:12] Claire (Mercantile SecOps): Yep, loud and clear. Claire here. Alex on compliance, Jamal joining a bit late but on.
[00:19] Jamal (Mercantile Infra): Sorry, joining now. Traffic was wild.
[00:22] Evan (Redwood SE): No worries. Quick plan: 20 minutes architecture, 20 minutes KMS/audit logs, last 30 minutes runbook and remediation items. Sound ok?
[00:31] Alex (Mercantile Compliance): That sounds fine. We have SOC2 in Q3 and want to make sure evidence points are obvious.
[00:36] Nina: Great. Evan, can you share the whiteboard?
[00:40] Evan: Sharing now. Ok, so first slide - private deployment topology. We propose a private control plane in Mercantile's VPC that talks out to Redwood agents that sit on your GPU nodes. There's no public egress from the model runners except to an approved egress-proxy.
[01:02] Claire: When you say 'agent', is that a sidecar or a managed binary? I want detail because of runtime hardening.
[01:09] Evan: It's a containerized runtime we deploy as a service on the cluster. Think of it like a lightweight serving shim. We do support a sidecar mode and a daemonset mode; for air-gapped or high-control shops customers pick daemonset + hostNetwork off.
[01:24] Jamal: HostNetwork off is important. We need to keep node network namespace separate. Also, can we pin outbound to a single NAT egress host so we can do IP whitelisting?
[01:34] Evan: Yes. Our recommended pattern is egress-proxy in your VPC — either envoy or an HA proxy — that is the only path to external services. Model runners only talk to the control-plane endpoints and to the egress-proxy for fetching things like updated model bits if allowed.
[01:50] Claire: And for telemetry and logs? We want verdicts — like who requested what, which model version, prompt hash, and retention windows tied to retention policy. How do you get audit logs out?
[02:02] Samir (Redwood SE): We emit structured audit events locally to a write-ahead log, and also stream to customer telemetry collectors via the egress-proxy. In a private deploy the customer picks the collector — e.g., Splunk/Datadog/S3 bucket — and we sign each event with a request trace id. There's a small caveat: the local WAL is ephemeral unless you configure persistent storage for the agent.
[02:27] Alex: For SOC2 evidence, ephemeral logs are tricky. We need long term retention — 12 months at minimum — and tamper evidence. Can we route logs to our internal S3 with server-side encryption and object lock?
[02:40] Evan: Yes, absolutely. Customers usually set up a bucket under their ownership and we push to it via the egress-proxy. For tamper resistance you can add object-lock and cross-region replication. We also support signing the events with an HMAC using a customer-managed key.
[02:54] Claire: About keying - you mentioned HMAC and K M S. Do you support Bring Your Own Key and HSM-backed keys?
[03:01] Nina: Short answer: yes. We integrate with common cloud K M S providers and also have an HSM option for Private on-prem packs. Evan can run through the handshake flow.
[03:11] Evan: Right. The control plane stores an encryption envelope key; the actual data keys for token caches and any persisted artifacts can be wrapped with your K M S. For cloud K M S we support AWS K M S, GCP K M S, and Azure Key Vault. For on-prem we can integrate with a PKCS#11 H S M or a customer H M S broker. The config uses a key-metadata entry so the operator can rotate keys without re-encrypting large objects — we keep track of key versions.
[03:42] Jamal: Rotation is critical — auditors will ask for rotation policy and a recent rotation event. What does rotation look like? Is it zero-downtime?
[03:49] Evan: We try to make it seamless for the running system: we rotate the wrapping key and record the rotation event in the audit log. Active sessions keep using cached unwrapped keys in memory until they expire. For full rewrap of persisted tokens we provide a background rewrap job that you can schedule during a maintenance window.
[04:06] Alex: We also need proof that keys were only accessible to the KMS principal we defined. Can you show the principals and KMS usage logs during the audit?
[04:13] Samir: We surface K M S usage events in the audit feed — which principal called decrypt/unwrap — and we can add correlation ids. If you use cloud K M S, the cloud provider's own audit logs (CloudTrail) will have the canonical record; we recommend crosschecking both.
[04:29] Claire: Ok good. Next, ingress: we want no inbound connections to the model runners from the public internet. How does Redwood handle admin/control plane traffic?
[04:37] Evan: Admin/control plane traffic goes through the private control plane endpoint inside your VPC (an internal ALB/NGINX) — it's not reachable from public internet if you set it as internal. There's also a mTLS mutual-auth channel between control plane and agents so credentials aren't just bearer tokens.
[04:53] Jamal: mTLS is important. Do you support cert rotation and short lived certs?
[04:58] Evan: Yes. Certificates for agent identity are short-lived by default (24 hours) and we have an automated renewal flow. You can also integrate with your internal PKI.
[05:07] Claire: On RBAC and SSO — we use Okta and have strict groups. We need mapping between Okta groups, RBAC roles in Redwood, and auditable actions.
[05:17] Nina: We support S S O via SAML and OIDC. You can map group claims to roles; we persist the role mapping change in audit logs and we have an API to fetch role assignments historically. Evan, do you want to expand?
[05:28] Evan: The mapping is fairly straightforward — group claim -> role id -> permission set. Every role change is an auditable event. For customers that want stricter separation, we support just-in-time provisioning turned off and require SCIM sync for user provisioning.
[05:41] Alex: For SOC2 we will need who changed RBAC mappings and when — plus an approval flow. Do you have an approvals integration?
[05:48] Samir: Not as an out-of-the-box workflow, but you can wire approvals into your ticketing system (Jira/ServiceNow) and we ingest the ticket id as part of the role-change API call — that becomes part of the audit event.
[05:59] Claire: Let's talk egress policies: we want to limit outbound to only three destinations — cloud K M S endpoint, internal telemetry collector, and our artifact mirror for model pulls. How restrictive can the egress policy be?
[06:12] Evan: You can lock it down to IP ranges and DNS names at the proxy. Typical customers use an envoy proxy with strict listener filters and a rule set that allows only those FQDNs/IPs. We recommend using FQDN + DNS resolution from a trusted resolver to avoid easy bypass.
[06:28] Jamal: DNS egress is a risk vector. We block external DNS from nodes and route DNS to an internal resolver. Does Redwood need to do any DNS lookups?
[06:36] Evan: Only for fetching model artifacts if you opt-in to auto-update. Otherwise all artifacts are pulled from your artifact mirror address which is resolvable internally.
[06:45] Claire: Regarding firewalling - do you have a minimal iptables/ufw baseline we should apply to the nodes?
[06:50] Samir: We have a hardened baseline for our agent nodes we can share — it's basically deny-by-default with allowed outbound to the egress-proxy, allowed inbound from the control-plane subnet on mTLS ports, and the Kubernetes control ports allowed from your admin jump host. We'll attach the sample in the runbook.
[07:06] Speaker 4 (unlabeled): Quick interjection — are there any tradeoffs for latency when using an egress-proxy for fetching model weights?
[07:12] Evan: There is an extra hop but in practice for model pulls it's fine because pulls are cached in your artifact mirror. For runtime token calls we keep the hot path inside the VPC and there should be negligible impact as it's just a local TCP connection to the proxy.
[07:26] Claire: About telemetry and PII — our compliance team wants to ensure prompts or user-provided content never leave our VPC in plain text. Can Redwood guarantee that?
[07:36] Nina: We treat content as customer data. In private deploy all traffic remains in the VPC unless you configure an external endpoint. We provide guards to avoid accidental outbound, and you can enable request-scrubbing before logs are sent out.
[07:50] Alex: Request scrubbing is good but we need to show in the audit that redaction rules ran and a sample of scrubbed vs raw events. Can that be part of the evidence bundle?
[07:59] Samir: We can include redaction markers and a checksum that proves a scrubber executed. We don't keep raw PII if you opt for scrubbing, but we can provide a proof-of-execution artifact that ties the scrub run id to the event ids.
[08:12] Jamal: For data residency, some of our customers are EU-only and we have to ensure the model runners never leave the EU region. Can the control plane pin to a region?
[08:20] Evan: Yes — in private deploy you control the region where the agents run. We also support a regional control plane. For hosted Redwood we have region selection, but for Private it's under your control.
[08:31] Claire: Ok good. Let's cover incident response: if there's a suspected exfil event, what are the immediate primitives we have?
[08:40] Evan: You can flip a global flag at the control plane to put all agents into read-only mode and block external egress. You can also revoke the agent certificate and rotate the K M S wrapping key which will force agents to fail crypto operations until re-provisioned. Both actions are auditable and write to the audit feed.
[08:58] Alex: Do you have a playbook or runbook for that? Auditors like to see the steps and timelines.
[09:04] Nina: We'll share a draft runbook that includes the CLI/API commands and sample tickets. That's one of the next steps.
[09:11] [10:00] Evan: (shares sample runbook) Step 1: isolate subnet / remove route to NAT; Step 2: set agents to read-only via control plane API; Step 3: revoke certs and rotate KMS; Step 4: gather audit logs and preserve S3 objects with object lock.
[10:22] Claire: This is helpful. A few nitty-gritty items from auditors: time synchronization (NTP) across agents and control plane for log ordering; signed timestamps; and clear chain of custody for logs.
[10:35] Samir: We recommend provisioning an internal NTP/Chrony pool and ensure agents are configured with that, and we also sign events with a timestamp authority token so you can prove ordering.
[10:47] Jamal: Network egress testing - can you provide a small valve test that we can run in our staging to validate only the allowed IPs are reached?
[10:55] Evan: Yes. We'll provide a small e2e test that fires sample model pull, telemetry emit, and KMS unwrap calls and reports which endpoints were touched. It uses mtr and tcpdump as part of the test harness.
[11:12] Claire: On the topic of SSO, we prefer group scoping via SAML, but we require that RBAC changes have a two-person review for production role changes. Can that be enforced?
[11:22] Evan: Not enforced natively, but you can use a policy agent that intercepts role-change calls; alternatively, you can put the role-change path behind a change-control service and only allow a service principal to call it once approvals recorded. We'll include a pattern doc for that.
[11:39] Alex: For encryption at rest of KV cache, token caches and model shards — where are those keys stored and are shards encrypted?
[11:48] Samir: Token caches are in memory and optional on-disk caches are wrapped with a data key that is wrapped by your K M S. Model shards are typically stored in your artifact mirror and should be encrypted with SSE or client-side encryption depending on your controls.
[12:02] Jamal: If we use client-side encryption for shards, do you support streaming decryption on the agent?
[12:08] Evan: Yes, the agent can stream-decrypt with a local key material provider if you install the key access plugin. We support a plugin API for that.
[12:18] Claire: Audit log retention - we want to be able to pull a bundle for a given date range and hand it to auditors. How heavy is that operation?
[12:26] Samir: We have an export API that can package logs for a date range, sign the bundle, and optionally encrypt it to your key. Depends on volume — could be a few GBs. We'll show a sample export.
[12:38] Nina: Quick pause — I want to call out a few typical follow-ups: 1) provide runbook and baseline firewall configs, 2) provide egress-proxy sample (Envoy/HAProxy), 3) K M S integration diagram and example rotation timeline, 4) sample audit export showing signed timestamps. Does that capture it?
[12:56] Claire: Yes. Also want a note on least-privilege IAM roles for the control plane and a list of permissions you recommend.
[13:03] Evan: We'll add an IAM cheat sheet for the cloud providers.
[13:08] Jamal: One more: can you explain how model rollback works if we detect a quality/regression issue? This is more ops, but we need to know how version pinning interacts with deployment policies.
[13:18] Samir: For private deploy you can pin nodes to a specific model artifact; control plane supports canary rollout across nodes and an automatic fallback if the model fails a health check. Rollback is instant if you trigger the policy.
[13:30] Alex: Final governance question: will Redwood sign any SOC2 addendum or will that be via a standard data processing addendum?
[13:39] Nina: We usually execute a DPA and can provide SOC2 reports for hosted services; for Private deployments we provide a package of evidence and a signed statement of responsibilities in the SOW. Legal will be involved.
[13:51] Claire: Ok, thank you. Let's move to the live demo checklist - Jamal and I will schedule a staging run with your SE.
[13:58] Evan: Great — we'll need network creds to provision a test agent in staging, and we'll coordinate an egress test.
[14:05] Nina: I'll follow up with calendar invite and include runbook links.
[14:10] Alex: Anything from your side on competitors? We heard VertixCloud pitches a fully managed private option that still puts some metadata on their control plane which we're cautious about.
[14:20] Nina: That's a key difference — our private deploy gives you full control of telemetry destinations and you can run the control plane inside your VPC. We'll include a short comparison doc.
[14:30] Claire: Great. That covers most. Jamal, anything else?
[14:35] Jamal: No, thanks. We'll validate NTP and object lock in staging.
[14:40] Nina: Cool. We'll close with quick recap.
